title: Pico de Gallo
subtitle: Fresh tomato, onion, chilli, and coriander salsa
excerpt: A fresh, uncooked salsa of diced tomatoes, white onion, jalapeño, coriander, and lime juice. The standard Tex-Mex table condiment. Best made with ripe tomatoes and eaten within a few hours.
sourceNotes: Pico de gallo: a Mexican fresh salsa (salsa fresca) served as a condiment across Mexico and Tex-Mex cuisine. The name means 'rooster's beak' in Spanish. One of the most widely eaten condiments in Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking, documented in American cookbooks from the 1960s. Based on classic Mexican and Tex-Mex sources.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made 15-30 minutes before serving so the flavours develop. Don't make more than 3-4 hours ahead; the tomatoes release liquid and it becomes watery.

content.text: Pico de gallo is a fresh uncooked salsa: diced tomatoes, white onion, jalapeño, coriander, and lime juice. The quality depends entirely on the tomatoes; use the ripest ones available. In summer, vine tomatoes or heritage varieties work best. In winter, cherry tomatoes tend to have better flavour than large salad tomatoes. Remove the seeds and liquid from the tomatoes before mixing. They make the salsa watery.

items.prepNote: ripe — seeds squeezed out, flesh finely diced
finely diced and rinsed under cold water, then squeezed dry
finely chopped; remove seeds for less heat

content.text: The dice size matters: all vegetables should be roughly the same small size, about 5 mm cubes or slightly smaller. This gives even flavour distribution in every spoonful.
Halve the tomatoes and squeeze out the seeds and liquid. Finely dice the flesh into 5 mm cubes. Put in a bowl.
Finely dice the red onion. Put in a sieve and rinse under cold water for 30 seconds, then squeeze dry in your fist. Add to the tomatoes.
Add the finely chopped jalapeño and coriander. Squeeze over the lime juice. Season generously with salt.
Stir and taste. Adjust salt and lime juice. Leave to sit for 15 minutes before serving; the flavours develop and soften.

items.symptom: Salsa very watery after a few minutes
items.cause: Tomato seeds and liquid not removed, or salted too far in advance
items.fix: Always deseed the tomatoes. Salt draws out moisture; make pico de gallo no more than 1 hour before serving, and add the salt in the final step.
Rinse diced onion under cold water and squeeze dry. This removes the harsh volatile compounds without removing the flavour.

items.symptom: Tastes flat despite all the components
items.cause: Under-salted or under-limed, or tomatoes not ripe enough
items.fix: Add more salt and lime juice, then taste again. Flavour develops as it sits. Ripe tomatoes are non-negotiable; the best salsa from poor tomatoes still tastes of poor tomatoes.
For a milder pico, remove the seeds and white pith of the jalapeño. That's where most of the heat lives. The jalapeño flavour remains without most of the burn.

content.text: Pico de gallo is the most widely eaten fresh salsa in Mexico and the most common table condiment in Tex-Mex restaurants. The name means rooster's beak; the origin is debated, but the salsa predates European contact. It relies on fresh ingredients and is best in summer when tomatoes are ripe. It goes alongside every taco, every nacho, and most other Tex-Mex dishes.
